patterns.text: Every ladder has a word with two vowels in it.

premises.text: Each step changes exactly one letter.
premises.gap: Without this stone, a step could change two letters at once, and the vowel could jump from the third place to the second in one move.

premises.text: Every word on the copyists' list has a vowel (a, e, i, o, u or y).
premises.gap: Without this stone, a word with no vowel at all could sit in the middle of a ladder, and the vowel could vanish and come back somewhere else.

premises.text: In "ship" the only vowel is in the third place. In "dock" the only vowel is in the second place.
premises.gap: Without this stone, we do not know that the vowel has to move at all.

premises.text: All four ladders on the table have such a word.
premises.why: Four ladders are a good reason to look for a proof. They are not the proof: the next ladder has not been made yet.

premises.text: Nasir has copied hundreds of ladders and never seen one without it.
premises.why: Nasir laughs. 'My memory is not a rule of the game. Leave me out of the arch.'
True often, but it does not hold any stone up. The arch needs only what the rules of the game say.

chain: Since each step changes one letter, and every word has a vowel, a word with only one vowel can lose that vowel only if the same step puts a vowel somewhere else. One step cannot do both. So the vowel can never move from the third place to the second while each word has one vowel. The vowel does move, because ship and dock put it in different places. So some word on every ladder must hold two vowels for a while.

scope.text: Every possible ladder has at least one word with two vowels.
scope.reply: Nasir nods. 'That is all the arch holds up, and it holds it for every ladder anyone will ever make, here or in a thousand years.'

scope.text: Every possible ladder has a word with two vowels side by side in the middle.
scope.reply: Nasir taps the arch. 'Look at the stones again. None of them says where the two vowels sit. On our table they always sat in the middle. That part is still a guess, waiting for its own proof, or for a ladder that breaks it.'
